newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish T-bill yields seen flat at primary tender.
newsitem.headline: Polish T-bill yields seen flat at primary tender.

text.p: Polish T-bill primary yields were expected to hold flat at Monday's 650 million zloty primary tender, as the finance ministry was seen reluctant to accept lower prices despite expected low demand, analysts said.
"The finance ministry does not plan to offer more (paper) and to allow prices to fall," said Piotr Korcz, a T-bill dealer at Bank Handlowy.
Analysts said the banks would not bid for more than 300-400 million zlotys worth of the bills because of a tight interbank deposit market.
They said that higher inflation expectations were also likely to limit demand.
In a December monthly Reuter poll of top Polish banks, analysts raised their year-end inflation prediction to 18.84 percent from last month's forecast of 18.71 percent.
At the last auction the finance ministry sold a total of 117 million zlotys worth of the bills after banks bid for 462 million zlotys against a 1.1 billion zloty offer.

Analysts said the finance ministry was able to cut today's offer to 650 million zlotys from an earlier planned 850 million to prevent prices from falling following strong sales of one-year and three-year bonds.
"The finance ministry cut its offer as its needs were probably covered in part by inflows from one-year and three-year bonds bought by the public," Handlowy's Korcz said.
The demand driven by corporate orders was expected to focus on shorter paper as banks were likely to hold back from opening positions.

"The money which will be invested in shorter papers would come from corporates as banks are reluctant to open positions with such high cost of short term financing," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski from ING Bank in Warsaw.

One-day deposits were bid at about 21 percent and the central bank signalled last week it wanted market rates to hold above 21 percent by raising its reference one-day reverse repo rate to 21.30 percent against 19.16 percent previously for 14-day operations.
Foreign investors were expected to stay sidelined as the zloty held relatively strong against a basket of currencies at 2.9 percent from the parity rate.
